title: Why Sierras de Málaga tastes the way it does

lede.text: Europe's most southerly mountains rise in this zone, and their spurs run south to the Mediterranean. Ripening temperatures stay moderate, with a drop at night, because the heat of the latitude is held in check.

chapters.title: Europe's southernmost mountains
paras: The zone sits at the lowest latitude of the European Mediterranean arc, right where it opens to the Atlantic. The vineyards grow in the Sierras de Málaga, the southern foothills of the Penibética range, the most southerly mountains in Europe.

Mountain makes up most of the province. A chain runs east to west from the Serranía de Ronda to the Sierra de Tejeda and Almijara, and its spurs run south to the Mediterranean. Flatter land is limited to the Depresión de Antequera in the north, the Depresión de Ronda in the northwest, the Jimena depression near Manilva in the west, and the river valleys, above all the Guadalhorce.

The vines do not form one block. They sit in patches of various sizes across the province, and the holdings are generally small because the terrain is so rough. The wider zone has six named areas, and the Serranía de Ronda is a subzone of its own.

fly.caption: The mountain complex at the eastern end of the chain.

chapters.title: Sunny days, moderate ripening
paras: The climate is Mediterranean, with dry summers and few rainy days. Depending on the area it takes on a temperate, continental or subtropical character. The zone's position and the way the mountains face the Atlantic fronts give an annual rainfall that is optimal for vines, though it is unevenly spread across space and time.
Sunshine hours are very high, as you would expect this far south. That sun favours musts with a high natural alcohol level. The wines from overripe grapes need such musts.

Even so, temperatures during ripening are characteristically moderate, with falls at night. The warmth of the latitude is held back both by the zone's position in a climatic transition and by local pockets of climate. The mountains and the sea create many of them. Ripening temperature matters a great deal here, because it shapes the range of aromas and the quality of the polyphenols, the molecules behind colour and structure.

chapters.title: Slate in the east, limestone in the west
paras: Soils are generally of medium to low fertility. North of the mountain arc the base materials are soft: sands, marls, limestones and sandstones. South of it they are more compact: mainly schist, slate, phyllite, gneiss and even marble.

Each area has its own twist. The Axarquía and the Montes de Málaga have slate soils. The Serranía de Ronda has limestone, generally with calcarenites. Around Manilva the soils are albarizos with a high limestone content, and the north has deep, brown-limestone soils.
In general the soils drain well, through their composition, texture or slope. Together with the modest fertility, that enhances the concentration of aroma compounds and the finesse of the wines.

fly.caption: Around Manilva the soils are albarizos, with a high limestone content.

chapters.title: Many grapes, four kinds of wine
paras: Phylloxera broke up and shrank the vineyards, and much of the province's great range of grape varieties was lost. The local ways of making wine from these grapes held on, among them dry and sweet reds. The first rules of the Málaga denomination, published in 1937, included the wine types "Rome Tinto" and "Tintillo de Málaga". In the early 1980s the tradition began to recover, and growers brought back old white and red varieties alongside others that had been planted locally.

The list of grapes is long. Whites can use Chardonnay, Moscatel de Alejandría, Pedro Ximénez, Sauvignon Blanc and Verdejo, among others. Reds include Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah, Tempranillo, Tintilla de Rota and Rome.

The wines are white, rosado (rosé) and red, and a fourth type is a sweet red from overripe grapes. Whites run from pale yellow to old gold. Rosados run from onion skin to a reddish pink with ruby tones. Reds run from violet to tile red. Acidity is always noticeable. Alcohol runs from medium to high.

The sweet red needs at least 15% total alcohol and at least 45 g/L of sugar. No wine may be sweetened or have its natural alcohol raised artificially. Both the alcohol and any residual sugar must be natural.

Yields are capped at 12,000 kg per ha for white grapes and 9,000 kg per ha for red, which is 84 hl and 63 hl of wine per ha. In the Serranía de Ronda the cap is 9,000 kg per ha for both. There the harvest must be by hand, in boxes of at most 30 kg.
A wine from a winery in the subzone can name it if all the grapes come from there. A wine from a winery in one of the areas can name that area if 85% of the grapes come from it.
